## The idea

Play C-F-G-C with every chord in root position. The harmonic route is clear, but
the upper parts leap whenever the root moves. Revoice the same progression so
that common tones remain and the other notes travel by small steps. The chords
then reveal another identity: four melodies moving together.

*Voice leading* is the shaping of those individual lines. A four-part texture
can be stored as soprano, alto, tenor, and bass arrays, which preserves each
voice's history across chord boundaries. Small total movement is a useful first
objective, provided the system also rejects crossed voices and respects range
and required tones. The problem is therefore closer to constrained optimisation
than to choosing four independent chord symbols.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 72
use_synth :piano

define :play_lines do |lines, muted|
  lines.each do |name, pitches|
    next if name == muted
    in_thread do
      pitches.each do |pitch|
        play pitch, release: 1.6, amp: 0.55
        sleep 2
      end
    end
  end
  sleep 8
end

naive = {
  bass: [48, 53, 55, 48], tenor: [60, 65, 67, 60],
  alto: [64, 69, 71, 64], soprano: [67, 72, 74, 67]
}

led = {
  bass: [48, 53, 55, 48], tenor: [55, 57, 55, 55],
  alto: [60, 60, 59, 60], soprano: [64, 65, 62, 64]
}

define :movement do |lines|
  lines.values.sum do |pitches|
    pitches.each_cons(2).sum { |a, b| (a - b).abs }
  end
end

puts "naive movement: #{movement(naive)}"
puts "led movement: #{movement(led)}"
play_lines naive, nil
play_lines led, nil
[:bass, :tenor, :alto, :soprano].each { |name| play_lines(led, name) }
```

Both renderings contain the same C-F-G-C harmonies. In the led version, the tenor
returns from G through A to G and then holds that G across the final boundary;
C remains in the alto where the next chord permits it. The whole texture is
smoother because the lines are smoother.
The muted passes then remove one voice at a time, making it easier to follow the
remaining paths without altering their pitches or timing.

## Change one thing

1. Move the led soprano's G-chord note from 62 to 74. The added octave raises the
   movement score and draws the ear toward one conspicuous jump, even though the
   chord's pitch classes remain unchanged.
2. Exchange tenor and alto on one chord. The vertical harmony survives, but the
   lines cross. Listen for the moment when their identities become harder to
   trace from one event to the next.
3. Mute each voice in turn. Identify which chord loses a root, third, or leading
   tone, then compare which absence alters the cadence most. Distance alone does
   not tell you which pitch performs the more important function.

## Why it works

`movement` adds the absolute pitch differences between consecutive notes in
each line. A lower result means less travel in this controlled example, but the
number is a cost function rather than a theory of good writing. A fuller search
must also reject crossing, keep each voice within range, preserve required chord
tones, and perhaps reward contrary motion at a cadence.

Storing lines first changes what the program can answer. A chord list describes
the pitches present at one moment. A voice matrix also records where each pitch
came from and where it goes next. Transpose that matrix and you can recover the
vertical chord view, but you have not thrown away the horizontal histories.

Lesson 27's greedy search chose the cheapest next chord at each boundary. A
global search can assess the entire progression before deciding. A locally easy
choice may leave no smooth route to a later chord, while a slightly larger move
now may lower the total. Four voices with a bounded candidate set are still
small enough for exhaustive enumeration, so the trade-off can be inspected
rather than guessed.

Common tones also affect articulation. Zero movement already reduces the score,
but holding a note through a boundary is not acoustically identical to striking
it twice at the same pitch. The current renderer reattacks every event and hides
that distinction. A more faithful version could merge equal adjacent notes in
one line, allowing a sustained tone to bind the changing harmony around it.

## Take it further

Generate every inversion of C-F-G-C that fits fixed bass, tenor, alto, and
soprano ranges. Reject candidates with crossings or missing chord tones, then
score each complete four-chord path by total movement. Play the cheapest path
beside the root-position baseline. Print both totals and all four resulting
voice arrays so a low score can be checked against the musical constraints that
gave it meaning.
